blocks.x: One, two, go, testing, okay. This interview with Curtis Mitchell and today's date is April 2nd, April 2nd, 1996. Okay. And we're at Tulane University. Okay. If you can get up to the mic. Curtis, let's start with your, you know your name and your birthday.
Well, my name is Curtis Daniel Mitchell. Okay. Well, I was born November 17th, 1926.
And where were you born?
I was born in New Orleans, up in the uptown Colton section, 1909 General Orgin Street.
Okay, General Orgin.
Yeah, that's between corn and spruce.
Okay, were you born in your house? Yeah. You were born at the house, okay.
Born in the house.
Did they tell you anything about your birth?
Well, it was, I'm one among seven. My mother had seven children. I was, uh...
Could you give me their ages and their, from the eldest to the youngest, and where you fit in?
Yeah, well, uh, I'm not really sure of my oldest sister age. She's the oldest. Okay. First born. I think she should be about 74 years old, I think.
Okay.
Her name is, uh, Annie Mae Mitchell at that time. She's married, you know. Okay. My next brother was Emil Mitchell.
Right.

And, uh, he's born 1923. He should be around 73 or something like that. My next brother, which is Ulysses Mitchell, he's a year and six months older than me. He's 70 now, he'll be about 71 this coming May, you know. So that makes me in the fourth born, you know. Which makes me in the middle of the family. Yeah. It's three older than me and three younger, you know. By the way, it's, uh, it's five of us still surviving.
Joe's still living?
Still living. Mm-hmm. And the two youngest ones is the ones that's gone, you know. As a matter of fact, I just bet a brother in February, you know.
Which one?
Which one? He's the one that's, uh, my younger brother. You know, he's the last boy that was born. But it was a girl after I, after I was born, it was a girl.
Yeah. Yeah.
And then him, the one that's died. And then the sister, which was the youngest. Well, she's, she's been there since 1978. My youngest sister.
Most of the kids born at home? Every all of us born in a house.

Did you? We all had midwives. There wasn't, there wasn't no, there wasn't no hospital. We were all born 1909, John Orkin Street. Okay. It was a, it was a large house. It wasn't too large. It was a down and up fourplex house. It was a large yard. We had a whole lot of yard. And the house sat way back in the yard. It was a full place, but in each apartment it was just a room and a kitchen, you know. We had a lot of yard to play in. We had palm trees in the yard. We had fig tree, chine ball tree, and peach tree. Peach used to grow real big in the yard. And, but we had no, no electric, you know. It wasn't the electricity?
It had no electricity.
No, we had, no weird lamps. Cooler lamps. Cooler lamps.
Cooler lamps. What about indoor plumbing?
Yeah, they had, they had a zinc and a, and a, and a faucet and zinc. But we had no bathtub. We had to all take a bath in one of those big, galvanized, number 10 I think, tub.
A tub? Yeah. Y'all would, y'all would take turns? I mean it was a. Yeah. I mean every.

My mother had the warm water on us. They stove, we had a wood stove, you know. Me and my brother, when I got, you know, like what, eight, seven to eight, nine years old. Six, seven years old. We had to go to the Bach factory over in Jefferson Parish. In Jefferson Highway they got, where they turn in in the road, they had a box factory.
Right.

And they had a picker factory behind that one. Yeah. We used to go up there and get wood from the box factory and bring. You know, and during those times, like if you got a wooden fence, those guys would steal the wood off your fence, you know, and burn it, you know. Right. Yeah. Sometime the coal man would pass, we'd buy coal from him and all that, you know. But she had the warm, you know, water.
Right.
For us to be, you know. Yeah.

Did you know, what, what, what, do you know when your mother and father were born? When they, when they, I mean, what, I mean, what, yeah, what their history is? Like when your father was born on his, if you look at his side?
Well, I don't know the actual birth date, but I think, I think my brother told me, Ulysses, he told me, the one little older than me, he told me that my dad was born in 1886, you
know. Where, and where?
In Pinecombeet Parish, you know, New Road. New Road. And, I don't really know when my mother was born, but I know my father was 17 years older than she was.
Where, what was her name? What was your mother's name? Rosa, R-O-S-A.
And what, what was your last name? Well, a man named Jackson.
Jackson, okay, Rosa. And when they married, well, became Mitchell, you know.
Okay, yeah, that's. Yeah.
Did, were they, were they married here, or were they, were they both from Point Coupe, or what was?

No, from what I understand, they got married just after my older sister was born. Okay. You know, when they first got together they wasn't married, you know. But, but they were married here. Yeah, they was married here in New Orleans, you know. We all was born here.
Okay.
And I was thinking my mother was from over, across the river in McDonoughville, but my brother tells me she's, she was from Scotland, Scotlandville, or Scotland or somewhere. Scotlandville?
Yeah. That's for the river.
Yes, that's where he is.
But your mother and father met here in New Orleans?
I think they met over in McDonoughville, you know. I think they. They, they used to be called it McDonoughville.
Now I don't know what they call it now. It's over, it's part of Gretna now. Yeah. It's all part of Gretna. Right. But your father was living over there and met her over there, obviously.

No, my mother was living over there and he, he met her, her over there. See, she was living over there with her father. You see my mother's, my mother, mother, which would be my grandmother, she died when my mother was a very young girl, you know. And so her dad married another lady named Miss Henrietta. Okay. And, well she had a stepmother, you know, and he's living across the river, you know, in McDonoughville, you know. Because when I was small, we used to, she took us over there a few times and my dad, my grandfather was over six foot, real dog man, you know, real built, you know. And he had a lot of chickens and, and things in the yard, you know. And he gave all us a little bit of chicken that we raised, you know. He had a yard full of them, you know. And we took them all, brought them all home and raised them and got attached to them, you know. And I remember the time when we didn't have nothing to eat, you know, the chickens that got grown, you know. And saying, you know. We didn't have anything to eat. And my mother went and killed one of those chickens and had them there sitting on the table, you know. And we had been playing, we had been playing with the chickens, give them nams and all, you know. Big Ben and all that. And we sitting there with the chickens there and none of us, we was hungry but we were going to eat it, you know. My mama said, why y'all not eating, you know. And we just couldn't eat them because we had been playing with them. We looked like they got part of us. You see like a seed got a chicken from the store or something, it might have been different.
You're not close to it.
Yeah. But we said, my brother said, man, why y'all not eating? I said, man, you go, I don't want to eat him. And we was hungry, you know.
Yeah. What was your father's name? We had a friend.
He's named Elijah. Elijah.
Nicholas Mitchell.
Elijah.
Nicholas Mitchell. Yeah. And he was from Pointe, from New Roads. Right. Did he talk a lot about New Roads or his family background in that era, in New Roads?

No, not to me he didn't, you know. You see, he might have talked, I got a lot of information from my brother Ulysses because, see, Ulysses was, looked like Ulysses was his favorite. Well he didn't tell none of us too much when we was younger, you know, about nothing. But after we got grown, you know, before he died he did most of talking to him. Matter of fact, my dad was, he's a very strict man, you know. Like when we were coming up, he wouldn't lie us out the yard or nothing and all that. I saw the guys be going to the movies and things and they'd have to come back and tell us how the movie was, you know, until I couldn't really go until I see him and my mother separated, you know, after that, you know. You know, and he was listening to me like he was a real mean person when I was coming up, you know.
Meaning what, why? To us, you know. I mean we used to get a lot of whippings.

Like for instance we had a dog, we used to call him Jelly Bean, you know. And my job was to keep the dog supplied with water, you know. Right. And like if one time like I forget or something and he come see the parent after the evening, whip me, you know. I'm talking about, you know, I like children whip me in children now, you know. Right. Yeah. And matter of fact, if, if they had 911, you know, like these kids calling 911 then, you know, child abuse, that my dad would stay in jail. Yeah. You know, with Steve, I think things change, you know.
So you didn't look at that he was really disciplining you, he was, it was.
Well in a way he was, but it looked like he was overdoing it.
You know what I mean? Yeah.
But he used to, when he whip us, he used to tell us too, say look, we shouldn't object to what he's doing because he'd rather do it than the police do it, you know. The police gonna do it, you know.
Oh, is that his attitude? That's what you see, yeah. Kind of his attitude of, if I don't do it, hey. Yeah.
The police might kill you and all that, you know.
So what better me do it than the police?
No, it's not that, in that sense.
In other words, what he's saying, he's whipping you but he's not gonna, you know, really kill

you or nothing, you know, or something like that, you know. But it seemed to me he treated me worse because my brother told me, and I'd ask my brother when I got wrong, I said look like, I said look like my, look like, we used to call him Nick, you know. We never did call him Dad or nothing, you know. You used to call him Nick?
Nick.
How that, well how that happened.
What do you think about that?

Well he, he, well he brought that on itself because see, from what I understand how that happened when my oldest sister was born. She was a little baby and just began to learn to talk. Matter of fact my mother told me this. And he told her, call her Rose, don't call her mother, you know. And she said look if you call me Rose, say I'm a whipping, you see, now you call him Nick. And so she started calling him Nick. And so all that's born after.
Start calling him Nick.
Yeah. So I really felt funny calling him Dad or something, you know. When he was older?
Yeah, yeah, we so used to doing it, you know. I'll call him Nick.

So what's happening? It looked like he was doubly hard on me because from what I understand my brother, I asked him, I said why I look like Nick was so hard on me that anyone would arrest him. He said because he really thought I wasn't his son, you know. Oh.
Yeah.

You know, he thought my mother would mess around on him or something, you know. But you know why? Because most of my other brothers and sisters, little shade lighted on him. I was the darkest in the family.
You were the darkest of the other family? Yeah.

They weren't really light. Right. But they lighted on me, you know. But what happened, he, when I went in the Navy and came on leave, my brother said, that's when he told him, he said, man, no, I'll never tell a woman that a child is not yours, see. Because since that brother went to the Navy and come back, he got all my features. And I really look more like him than the rest of them, you know. But when I was growing up, you know, he couldn't see this, you know. But by him being really hard on me, it looked like my mother landed more to me. Yeah. So I think I was her favorite, you know. Out of the group of the kids? Yeah, her favorite, because I guess he's saying I needed somebody, you know. And you know, that's what I say about all kids, they should have somebody, you know. But he was a smart man, though, you know. He, you know, he knowed how to do a lot of things, you know. What was his occupation?
What did he do for the living?

Well, he was, I would say, he's all around, because he could do anything with a house. He could build any kind of building. He could do repairs and all that, you know. And I remember the time he knew a lot about, he wasn't no doctor, but he knew a lot about curing people with things, you know. Because I remember they had a man just come to our house. I remember his name, his name was Mr. Sims. And the man had a big hole in his side there. And he had, he said he had been every doctor he could find, and he said he could find a cure for him, you know. My daddy used to, you see the way the house was, we would live in one side, which was the room in the kitchen.
It was just one big room in the kitchen?

Yeah, it was the room in the kitchen. See, it was the room in the kitchen, it was full place, the room in the kitchen on this side, one on this side. Right. One outside and one here. Okay. Well, they had some people living next door to us, we living upstairs. We living in the room in the kitchen, all of us.
So all of y'all lived in one room?

Rum in the kitchen, yes, yes. One big room. Yeah, and so what happened, the people next door moved. My daddy cut a wall on the other side so that gave us full rooms. You understand? Yeah. Well he could do that because the man, the landlord, he had my daddy in charge, had him collect the rent for him.
Oh, okay.

And he'd come collect until my daddy told me he wanted that side. So afterwards, he, the floor, like the kitchen here and the kitchen on this side, the room here and the room, he took the room in on the far side for his personal room, see.
Oh, I see.

And when he come out of the room, he locks it. We couldn't go in there. In other words, we all had three rooms to our room. Right. You know, two rooms in that kitchen on this side. Yeah. So what he would do, he had all that together, but it took time this man came, you know, and he'd bring the man in the room and they'd stay in there a while. I don't know what he'd do, tell me that. He must be treating him or something.
Yeah. But anyway, the man got killed, you know. Your father must have known some kind of folk medicine. Something, something.
I think.
Something he learned. It's a lot of things.
Growing up in Pointe-Pack. It's a lot of things that he died with, I think, that was secret that he could have helped the world, I think.
Yeah, well there's a lot of, there's a lot, two, I think. A lot of the folk remedies that people use. Yeah.

And that man, he used to lay around on Spruce Street, you know, on Spruce between Eagle and Monroe. And we used to, me and my brother used to pass there, and the man used to just dig in the pocket and give her two and three and five dollars. And say, your daddy saved me, you know. And man, dude, during that time, man, fifty cents to us was a lot of money. You know about two, three, five dollars, man. Yeah. You know? Yeah, man. And I learned that after he died, you know, he died when I was in the Navy, you know, in 1945. When he died, after he died I found out, him and my mother were separated then.
Right. Yeah.

You know. So, she went up there and she found out that he, he had all these things up here where he used to give abortions to women, you know, all this. Oh, really? Yeah, all that. He had all the equipment, the chairs with a little marmalade on and all that.
Your father, your father? Yeah.

Wow. He had all that, you know. And he could do anything with a house. He used to wait for those people, you know. A lot of houses he helped prepare down on St. Charles Avenue and the Altman Boulevard. He used to wait for those kind of people, you know. And see, that's another thing I didn't like about him. We around here, you know, like, we look like we're the poorest of the poor. But he used to do all that work, he used to make pretty good money and just carry around in his pocket, you know.
So you think he didn't, he just didn't carry around? No, no. What did your mother, did your mother work at all?

Yeah, he, when they were together, he didn't want her to work, didn't want her to go anywhere, you know, but to church and back, you know. But what happened, what happened was she worked after they separated, you know, but I'll get to that later.
Oh, okay.
When I was about, I'd say about six years old, when I was, we had a quartet group, you know. My brothers and I. What you sang?
Yeah.

That's my first encounter with music, you know. Now, I was the youngest in the group, and my brother Ulyss, and my brother Emile, and my sister was a leader, you know. I had another sister younger than me, and another brother, too, and you know, but they wasn't born, you know. Right. Right. Yeah. Oh. Sorry. No.

And so me and my brother used to go sit on the porch and listen at them, you know. And we'd listen, I'd listen at the tenor player, I mean the guy that sang tenor.
Well the singer, the singer. Yeah.

And he'd listen at the baritone part, my other brother listened at the bass part, my sister would listen to the lead. And so they was practicing one time and after they took a little break, well we started singing out there on the porch. We used to be on the porch listening at them inside. And then after a while they heard us singing and they came out there and said, was y'all singing?
He said, yeah. And they made us come in and sing with them, you know.
And so after that we decided so good until they started bringing us on some of their programs, you know. And we got to be very popular singing in those churches.
Now what was your group name? What was your group name? The Mitchell Four.

You called yourself The Mitchell Four. The Mitchell Four. I was about six years old then, you know. And we used to sing, you know, we wouldn't sing for no money or nothing, we just did it because we liked it, you know. But one time we were singing and they had a lady pick up some collection and she gave me the money, you know. I thought she meant for me to put it in the collection basket so I put it in there. And she said, I meant that was for y'all, you know. But anyway, we got to be very popular all up through Colton and one time we went to a church convention and slide there, you know, that's my first time being away from the mall, you know, small kid.
Slide, slide out.

Yeah, slide there. That didn't look like a long way then. Slide out and hammering, you know, we sung all through there for convention. And my dad, well that's the only time I seen him let my mother go that far without him. You know, he had to stay home with my little younger sister. And so we got pretty good, I think if we would have kept on, we might have really made it good,
you know. Did you enjoy singing in gospel? Oh yeah, yeah.
I loved that, you know.
Was that kind of a primary foundation for what you would develop later, music?
Yeah, I think so. But we were, see we were all music and inclined, but I'm the only one that really did it professionally, you know, they all played around the house. I'll get to that too.
Were your father and mother, did they encourage you or did they play music?
No.
Neither one?

No. I'mma tell you about that, see. But this thing with the quartet, one time, we were doing so good, you know, so people, they start paying us, giving us their money, you know. Like I said, we wouldn't ask for nothing but they volunteer, you know. And so one time they had a big thing, they had about ten, fifteen quartets. And we were the only kids, you know. All the rest was grown people, you know, grown men. And the people were there, looked like they all were there just to see us, you know. All the men, and I had a guard mother. And my daddy had said it was all right for us to go, you know. So, and then, see my mother used to cut out of hair, boy's hair. So this is the first time we had been to the bar, but we were sharp, you know. We were all ready to go. Everybody, you know, all pumped up. So at the last minute we go, they go and my daddy tells us, well, you all can't go. And man, that's a big disappointment to everybody. Everybody, oh man. And so ever since then, that's where we just scrapped the quartet, man.
Your father just wouldn't let you all go out?

No, we just got disgusted, you know. And see, but what happened before that, when we would rehearse, he tried to get in that with us, you know. He wanted to practice with us like he wanted to join the quartet. But he was making a discord, you know. We'd tell him, say, man, you're making us all mad, you know. But he couldn't sing. No, he couldn't fit in with us, you know. And I guess he got pissed by that or something. I don't know what it was either. You see my mother was going.
Maybe he was a little jealous.

Yeah, I think so. And see, my mother, when we go on the convention, she'd go with us and I guess maybe he'd figure, well maybe, I'm not that she might get a man or something, you know. He's jealous I think, you know. Yeah, it seems.
Yeah.

Yeah. So after that the quartet broke up, you man, but no telling how far we could have went, you know. You know what I mean? You might have been bigger than Jackson 5, the son of people, you know. Do you remember what songs you all used to sing?
What was in your repertoire of songs? When you sang?

Well we used to do all those spiritual songs, but then a couple of them, like one time we sang for, at our school, you know, they had a parent teacher meeting. And we sung for them, you know. And we, Our God, Thee, and all this, you know. All the spiritual songs, you know. Anything else?
Let's see.

Well anyway, I can't really think, you know. But anyway, we sang for the parent teacher meeting, and everybody enjoyed it. And so the next day when I went to school, you see we were all in the same school, but we were in different classes, you know. So a girl came in and said, Mr. Honey, Mr. Honey was the principal, you know. I said, Mr. Honey want to see Curtis Mitchell, you know. Well I know I had did nothing wrong, you know. I'm wondering what he wants. He wants me in his office. So when I go there, I see my brother Ulyss, he's there. And my brother Emile, he's there. And he tell us, he said, look, see I want you all to go in there and do, we're going to go in the bar of Charlie, I want you all to sing them songs that you all sung at the parent teacher meeting. So we told him, well Mr. Honey, see we can go in the bar of Charlie, but my sister can't go in there. She's a girl, you know. So he got some guy out another quartet that sings lead and he had us in the bar of Charlie singing for him, you know.
Were a lot of your peer groups, people your own age, were they singing quartets, singing in church?

Well they had about two, three quartets around our age up there, but they didn't compare with us, you know. Because one time we sang for a church and the woman had baked the cake for the best quartet, you know. But what happened, they called us a fish, you know. And so by the time they got to the, them other guys who were that singing, man, when they called them up, they wasn't there, they done snucked on out of the church, you know. So we got the cake, you know.
What school were you going to?

Yeah, I mean I know Danny White.

They're from around there? Yeah. The Leonidas.

Okay.
Yeah, I knew Danny had some gospel background but I didn't know all of them.
Yeah. But he never did sing that quartet.
His brothers was.

Reel 4 with Curtis Mitchell on April 2nd 1996. Follow through that with Guitar Slim you always got stuck with the driving. Yeah, when I would.
Let me spill the board. Real, I guess we're number five with Curtis Mitchell and it's April the 2nd, 1996. You're talking about Ralston Crawford. You remember Ralston Crawford?

Yeah I remember that man. And the reason why I remember him, because he used to be, look like a lot of places we played, you know, and why he stood out. During that time you didn't see many white people around that area, you know. Yeah I remember him. And he's a good show now while he was doing them pictures, you wouldn't think that they would be as bad as they is now, you know. You think well it's just a guy taking pictures, you know.
That's a good point. Did white people come to the Dew Drop?

They'll sell them man. I remember when Zachary Scott came there man, and they bused him, he went to jail. Him and Frank and all of them. Oh really? Just because he was a movie star, Zachary Scott. I'm quite aware of him I'd have told you about that.
No but I know I've got stuff from the newspaper. Yeah man, yeah.

But you were there that night? Yeah, they bused them all to jail man, Frank Pangea, all of them. You know. Because he was in there, he was just a white dude in a black club, that's all. You know. Yeah. So that was a problem. Yeah, right. All the man wanted to do is see the show. Yeah. But that was law or something. I don't know man. Yeah. Yeah. Well how I started playing bass man.
See I was. Yeah. Because it seemed like most of the, yeah. In fact I'm surprised you, all these other instruments because I know you was a bass player. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well piano was my first

Well anyway, I started playing bass. I was standing in the doodrop and I didn't have no job, you know. And the telephone rang in there and the bartender said, telephone for you. So I gets the phone and there's Raymond Montrell, Roy Montrell. He said, man, I need a bass player, man. I got a job at the Texas Lounge. The Texas Lounge was on Canal Street. Brass Rail was in the next block. He said, I got a job six nights a week. I need a bass player. You know I can find one? I said, no, man. He said, man, I can try that by. They said, look. I said, why don't you come on and make the gig? I said, man, I don't know how to play no bass. He said, man, you can play the gig so you look like a bass player. You know?
What does that mean?

That's what he said. What does that mean? I said, well, look, man. I said, I never had no experience with no bass. I tried to play nothing. I said, but just suppose I could play. I said, I don't have no bass. You see, that ain't no problem, see. I'm going to get one of Gerald Adams' basses. Gerald got three basses. He on the gig with one. I tried to get him, but he's working. So I'm going to borrow one of his other basses. He said, all you do is come down here and the bass will be on the Berenstain. So, man, I need a gig so bad. I said, well, I'm going to give this a try. So I go down there and there was the bass on the Berenstain. He was on the gig. He wanted to use me. He had Earl Baptiste on saxophone and Harry Nance on drums. You know? So what happened, man? I picked up the bass and they started playing. And I made it through the night, but I was going purely on air. I didn't know what I was doing, you know.
How did you keep up with it? I mean, physically, how did you...

Yeah, that's what I'm saying. Well, I just jested myself and he said, well, that wasn't too bad, man. So what happened? They had blisters rolled up on my fingers, on both fingers, with blisters, you know. Oh, man. And there's a lot of, you know, like that water coming in you. And so, man, I took a pen and I busted. I said, well, Lord, I said, I've got to play tomorrow night in my hands in this condition, you know? And I said to myself, well, I guess I've got to play until I get the calluses, you know. So what happened? I come back the next night and played, next night played. Each night I got a little battered. So when I made my... I used Jared's bass for three nights. And after that, I don't know if I remember Tate, blind Tate. I used Tate bass for the next street night, blind Tate. So what happened? When I made my first payday, I went down to Swab's Music Store. There's Swab's Music Store on Dry Street, you know. So I went to Swab's and I told a man, I said, man, I like to put some bass, bass fill, you know. So he tells me, he said, well, he said, you got any credit? I said, well, I don't have no credit. I said, everything I bought, I said, it's been cash, you know. He said, well, oh, I don't know how to let you have it. You ain't never had no credit. I said, look, man, I said, if I never had no credit, I could be buying things cash. I said, see, you can't say I got bad credit or good credit. I said, unless I get a chance. I said, I may have to establish some kind of credit. So why not start here, you know?
So he said, okay.

He said, well, what other job you do besides music? I said, well, this is all I do, I got now, the music right now. That's all I do. You don't know how to trust those musicians. You know, that's what he says, you know. I said, well, man, let's, I said, well, let's face it, man. I said, what kind of store is this? I said, this is a music store. I said, who else you gonna deal with unless it's a professional musician in the high school, band kids or something. So he said, oh, you got something there. So he went on and let me have the base. I gave him $25 on it, cost $336. I still got the base. Yes, I got it. And so I went on and paid him out before it was due time. And so that's how I established my credit, you know. So after that, I had this job six nights a week, man, with Montrella. Yeah, I sit down there, go to the wild with him, at the Texas Lions. Yeah, Lee Allen was playing in the next block with him and Earl Palmer with Paul Gaten band.
Yeah. What was that place? It was across the street.

No, it's on the same side of the street, but just in the next block. Yeah. Red Rail, man. And that's how I started playing bass, you know. But I never had a job playing bass like on the road. You see like I was on the road with Lloyd Price and I was playing. The only time I played bass was local. And lately I've been over in Europe. I played. I went to Finland, Helsinki, Franklin. I played there. And I played in Bangkok, Thailand. You know. And I went to Monte Carlo, but I didn't play bass there. I played my alto saxophone and brass band and then on stage too. You know.
So you played with Montrell at Texas Lounge. What year was this?
That was before I went on the road with Lee Allen. And then Silhouettes and Ruth Brown and Clyde McFadden, you know.
I'd say that was around, around in the 60s.

Around in the 60s. Early or mid 60s or something like that, you know. Man, it's kind of hard to relocate one of these times. I don't, I think that was before I was with Danny White, you know. Because I played with Danny White, you know. We played down at the Dream Room, then we played at the Show Bar and everywhere else around here, man.
Do you remember Danny White's band for a while, for Goodball?
I was playing with him. I'm playing on all his records. So young. Kiss Them All Goodbye and all of them.
Oh, okay.
And then I'm playing on Big Chief.
Well, I knew, yeah, I knew that you were on Big Chief before.
And then I'm playing on It Am I Fault with Smokey Johnson. Smokey.

Yeah. Was that the, I want to ask you something. How long did it take you like, when you were playing, to get proficient to where you felt like you really, you felt like you were a real bass player? Yeah. You must have taken your own.

Yeah, well after I, see I never took bass at Greenwald School. Yeah, mostly self-taught there, you know. So what happened, after I finished that gig with Montra, Texas Lodge, I went on the road. But I didn't go out there playing bass. I went out there playing piano with Clyde and them, you know. And then when I come back, well, during the time when I was playing with Montra, I already had bought a book, you know, and the bass. So when I come back I went to practicing out the book, you know, and I learned how to fang it. I learned to correct fang. Because the first night I played with Montra, when I got off the job, my fingers wasn't only swollen, man. It was all hurting for the fang and it's wrong. Now I don't know about my earbringer, it might have brought out good sounds, but I'm talking about physically, feeling, man. So after I learned the correct fang, I went out the books and I learned to bore a little, you know, and I kind of got it together.
So you think you taught yourself correctly?
Yeah, yeah, the book, you know. I learned the position.
You teach yourself, you teach yourself wrong sometimes.

Yeah, yeah. And how I started playing with Danny White, see, Danny White had a band, and they had Irvin Bannister, Ernest Hollins, Hulk, Henry Hawkins, the trumpet player. Henry Hawkins, yeah, Hawkins. Yeah, yeah. And Irvin Bannister and Joe Fox in the band, you know. And so he got this job on St. Charles Avenue with the club Sands, you know. And Danny said, man, I need a bass player, you know. And Ernest Hollins told him, so why not get Curtis, man. See, I was the last one in Danny's band. He had all the rest of those guys. And they learned a true year on piano. True year?
Leonard True year, yeah. True year, okay.
Cotton came later.
Well anyway.
Lawrence Cotton was in his band later? Yeah, he came later. Okay.
Just like when he got George Davis later and also Leo Nelson Taylor later.

And then he got Teddy Riley too. Well anyway, he told him to get Missy because man, this guy's the only player say he arranges too, you know. And so when I first got with the band Danny and them men, they looked like they couldn't play ABC, you know. And Ernest Hollins, they hadn't read no music since they left Booker T. Washington High School, you know. And the first arrangement I made for him, it was whole notes, whole notes were real slow notes and they was having trouble with that man, whole and half notes. One time when we were playing there, they had a guy that had a song on the box by Ray Charles. Let me see the name of this song.
It was in the early 60s? Yeah. Must be in the early 60s.
I Want a Little Girl to Da Da Da. I think that's it. Want a Little Girl to Love A Lot? Yeah.

I think that's T-Bone Walker. I Want a Little Girl, that's what the name of the song. Yeah but Ray was doing it. Yeah Ray was doing it. I think T-Bone, I remember you the first one did it. Yeah but I Want a Little Girl.
Yeah.
Well the guy used to play that a lot on the joke box, you know, and he asked Danny, could we do that, you know.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. I want a Little Girl to Love A Lot. Yeah. He said, man, see Danny bent on me, but he didn't, from the neighborhood, but he didn't know that I had the knowledge about music that I did, you know. He told me, he said, man I heard you can arrange. I said, yeah, he said, can you write this, the background for this? I said, yeah, I can write it. I said, but you got to bring me a record player, because I ain't got any player on where I live at. I ain't no record player. So he brought his record player over and he brought the four to five, you know. And I wrote it out, you know. On the staff music. I wrote it off the Cold Hill's record and wrote it on out for horns. We didn't have but two horns then. They had Hulk and Ernest Highlands, because Teddy hadn't got there. He had Teddy Riley. So I voiced it for two horns and the rest. And man, it come out beautiful. And we started playing with man. And so ever since then he used to bring me a record, like two, three, four weeks. And what did he do?
He'd come to my place I lived by myself.

And I said, hey, this record player there, and he'd bring the 45, or the album or whatever. And what I'd have to do, I'd have to, sometimes like a Jack Wilson song or something, it'd be too high or something, and I'd put it in his key. Yeah, I'd put it in the key, come for him to sing. And I'd arrange it. And it'd always come out fine, you know. And man, we got so popular. But them first few rehearsals had real problems, because they wasn't up on their reading, they hadn't read in so long. And then after the more they read, it come back to them. And so man, one time we was playing at the club saying, we got in a big fight with them white boys around there, you know. We got in a fight and so we lost a job. The man got mad and fired us. But they had another man out there at the Club Safari.
You know where Safari was? Yeah, Safari was.

He used to come around trying to get us all the time, but we didn't want to go, because you know. But after the Cat fired us, we started working out there. Making more money, man, and everything. You know. That one guy used to come around, man. That guy, man, used to, like when we'd knock off at the Safari, he'd have his girlfriend there and have us playing overtime because he'd keep filling the kitty with money. You know? Man, and see what happened, when I was around for Danny, I wasn't charging him nothing. So Ernest Holland told Danny, I said, well man, why don't you give Curtis the kitty? Yeah, that's the money.
The kitty.

The kitty. You know, that was coming, the kitty. So man, we was at the Club Sands. The kitty wasn't much, you know, but four or five dollars a night. But when this guy started coming every night, man, I used to bring home 70, 80, 100, 150 dollars a night, you know. Because sometimes the cat said, man, well, you're going to pay a little over. And you know, and them cats wasn't fucking, they wasn't getting nothing. So I said, well man, look, I'll pay you all for whatever. You know? So what happened, man? The cat was putting so much money in the kitty until Urban told him one night. He said, man, what kind of work you do? He said, well, I'm a counter. And the old one was just joking with him. He said, man, you must be juggling the books or something, you know. The cat laughed, you know. And man, he started putting so much money in there, Fox told Danny, he said, man, look, see, this is your band, see. See, the cat doing the random for him, see, we're going to have to start splitting the kitty, man, saying you've got to start paying the cat for your ram. I said, well that's fine with me, so I can pay you some kind of way, you know. But Fox said he wanted some of that money, you know. So man, right after that happened, guess what happened? He seen people the next day with a cat, about the next few days, after he had made that deal about, you know, me. Well this cat got busted for embezzlement, man. Oh, correct. You know, so I was in, that's Mr. Kitty. Well that's. So he left with Danny Stead to pay me, see. But man, this is going to show you what, what, what Irvin was joking about was true.
Uh-huh. It was true, yeah.

But guess what, the cat must have been so good to him, they bust him in, he didn't even do no time. But, and then he finally wind up getting his job back. But then he turned around and messed up again, did the same thing over again. Man.

Were you involved with any of Danny's hit records, hit records? Kiss DeMar, Goodbye, or? Yeah I'm playing on them. You're playing on Kiss DeMar? I'm playing on all his records. All of his records? All of them, yeah.
All of his records?
Yeah.
But I only did one recording for him. As an arranger?
Yeah, arranger.

I used to do all his copying, you know, like all, but as far as any recording I only did one, that was one called I Surrender. I got it in my band now, you know. I Surrender. The rest of them Wardell Cazell did. He did the Raymond on Kiss DeMar Goodbye and all the rest of his song.
And you were on Big Chief with Professor Longhead. Yeah, I was playing on the piano.
I always have a question about that song.

I think I was going to ask Wardell. I was going to ask Wardell this? That lick that Fess plays, you know, that he plays on the piano? Yeah. Now, did Earl write that or did Fess write that lick? Or did you know who wrote that lick? No, well, I think Fess just come up with that itself. You think so? Yeah. That's his style, I think. But what happened, man, Fess had us in the studio down there all night with that.

The recording it looked like almost because he's the only one who wasn't reading, you know. Well, see, Fess was supposed to originally sing it, but he couldn't sing it and play it at the same time where he was playing. And so Earl wound up singing it. That's Earl singing and whistling. So Earl just wound up singing it, you know. But then another thing with Fess, the man stopped Fess from playing his left hand. Because he's playing this one hand. Because see what he was playing with his left hand in the bass was interfering with the figure I was playing. It was interfering with that. And then he stopped, he put a pillow down there by his foot because he had to have the kick in the piano, you know. When he was playing at the Caledonia Inn years ago there at the upright piano, he kicked a spot in there. And you see them baby grinds, he kicked a pedal where the pedal come down, you know.
So I don't think he used the pedal at all. I don't think he used the pedal.
No, no. He kicked. And so what he was doing there was interfering with where Smoke was playing on the drum. So the man put a pedal down there, you know. But it all come out good, though.
Oh God, did it.

Now before Walter did a ramming on it, I had a ramming on it. You know. When I tried to get the cast together on it, man, I couldn't get them a rehearsal. And they think I know where I would and got Walter to do another ramming. Of course it wasn't the same thing. You know, the ramming wise, because you know two rangers don't think alike.
Well how did Earl bring the song to you? What did it sound like when Earl brought it?
Well he just, he sang it to me like the same way he sang it on there. But I put my eye there of how the horns were supposed to go.
So that's all you had heard was what Earl sang to you? He didn't have played on the guitar?
Yeah he'd play it and show me how it'd go and all like that, you know. You know. Yeah. I wish I had that around my mind. I don't know what happened, you know, if I had it, man.
Well how was it different from Waddell?
Well the horns, the bass figure was different, plus the horns was around different. Mine was just as effective as his, but you know you got the head to the hitch, you know.
Yeah, we love it.
I remember we rehearsing at the, they're the place called Blue Eagle on Felicity Street. We rehearsing at Big Airman and all of them was there, man.
The whole group was on their session?
No, no, not all of them, but a lot of them, you know. Because see this happened about a year or so before they recorded it, you know.
Earl already had the tune in his head. Yeah.
Yeah. Well man I lived on Louisiana Avenue, man.
Right, I remember when I first met you years ago, when I first met you living in Louisiana.

Yeah. And man we used to, all night long, we used to be fun with music. As a matter of fact, me and Earl had a company together there. What did you want? The recording, recording the company we were developing, you know, but it never did materialize, man. And man the police had to bend us our house a few times, about to stir it in a piece and all that mess, you know. Because we'd be there all night long with tape recorders and things, man. At your house or?
Yeah at my house.
At your house. At your house. Because we cut BB Daddy, remember BB Daddy? We cut him and we recorded him and we recorded the cat named Billy. Billy? Billy, yeah. Billy Jenkins.
Yeah I got them records too.
And Guitar Joe? Was Guitar Joe? Guitar Joe's around there, yeah. Yeah man.
And since you've got Guitar Joe in Longton, when Earl played the gig about six months ago, you know Guitar Joe, you've got Guitar Joe to open for him. Yeah.
Well Joe got a giant nine, he got a place of business. Joe?
Yeah. The Guitar Joe's guy?
Joe got a place on Drive and Seven. What is it? It's a ballroom, you know. Oh. Yeah. Yeah.
He was fixing calls, you know. Well I knew he was a jack of all trades.
Yeah he got a night job now, man.
So in the 60s how much more arranging did you do like for recordings, etcetera?
Well I did, I ran for quite a few people, you know. I don't get much, it looked like.
Much recording and work. Yeah. Yeah.

I'm doing some things for myself, I'm trying to get recorded, man. You know, I just haven't had the money to do nothing. But I've been writing on some things, you know. I played on a lot of other guys' stuff, but I never really did nothing for myself yet, you know, featuring myself, you know.
Well you think you've always been known as a side man. Yeah. I've always known Curtis Mitchell as a solid side man, you know. But never the front man, never the front guy.
Nah. Nah. Well see I play out there in the Continental every Sunday morning.
Is that the brunch thing?
Yeah, brunch every Sunday morning. I've been playing there for about eight, nine years now, with Greg, Greg Stafford. Yeah. Me and Greg, Michael White, and Steve Bailock on guitar.
And I do a lot of singing around there.
You know where before I wasn't singing, you know, since I started singing I said, well, I'm going to try to record something for me too.
When did you start, like really, was it the 60s when you got off the road and you started just doing gigs in New Orleans? Yeah. Doing mostly gigs in New Orleans. Yeah, right. Yeah.
So have you been doing mostly, what do you call it traditional?
Traditional, yeah. Most traditional, yeah. I've been getting most gigs now on bass.

And lately I've been getting a few gigs at the Preservation Hall, some on bass, and some on piano. You know I played last week on piano down there. At the hall? Yeah, Preservation Hall. And then they called me a few times to play bass too. But I played in almost every club down there on Bourbon Street. The Paddock Lounge and everywhere down there, man. As a matter of fact I don't really like to play on Bourbon Street no more because the hours are so long and sometimes I get a job paying two or three hours and make it more than I'm playing for five hours down there, man. You know? Yeah. Yeah. And then I'm drawing my Social Security. Then I get a check from the union too. You know, so. I'm really, I've really been waiting on this because I can practice when I want it. I ain't got to worry about paying a rent, you know? Yeah.
You mentioned Alan Toussaint and there was a song that you said you'd sing.
What's the new?
Yeah. Tell me that story about it.

Yeah, well he, whenever I see him, you know if he's around the piano he'll play what's new. And he'd tell me, he'd say, man, you remember you taught me how to play this song? He'd say I still play the same way you taught it to me. You know? What's new? Bob Crosby, remember him? Uh huh.
Yeah.

Well his bass player wrote that song. I forget his name. The guy used to play bass with him. What's new? It's a standard tune, you know? Yeah. But one time when he saw us come around and do drop, I showed him the charges.

Did you look at yourself in sort of a way, like with Alan, did you look at like, it's because you were old what, fourteen years, Bob? Yeah. And look with Earl and with Huey Smith, those kind of guys, did you look at yourself as a mentor in a way?
In a way, yeah.
That you were a good kid.
Yeah. They always, all of them are always respecting me, you know, as a musician, you know.
Well most of your guys, you were, I mean, who were a little older than, say, Earl and Alan, those people, did you all, was everybody really helpful to the younger guys in general?
Yeah. Yeah, man. Yeah. But man, I knew Earl was going to make it some kind of way when he can't push stuff, come around and drill and drive. He was ambitious and also Huey and Alan, man.
What do you mean ambitious? What do you mean Earl was ambitious?

Well he's always fooling with the music, you know, always interested, man. You know. Huey and all of them, you know. Yeah. Yeah. And then they used to have Boca, Boca started coming around there too with them.
Boca, yeah.
Yeah, man. And Boca and Alan used to play them organs in the dude drop, you know.
In an organ? Organ?
Yeah. I used to play piano but I didn't fool the organ. You know, they used to play the organ man, you know, in the dude drop, him and Boca. Yeah.
Boca was good, man. Oh, I want to ask you, you know, you played bass, but did you ever try electric bass? Yeah, well I used to play electric bass with Danny.

You played electric bass with Danny. When I first started when I was playing the violin, the bass violin. Right. And then I started playing electric, you know. Matter of fact, I see a guy now, he told me, he's a white guy, he's a bass player too. He told me, he said, man, you know you're the first guy I seen with electric bass, man, electronic bass. I look up there and seen you playing that, I thought it was another guitar. I said, no, man. What was the feeling about electric bass?
I mean, when that, when it came here?

Well, it's kind of different, the feel, but the string, the tuning up is the same, you know, but the feel of it is, it's different, you know. Well, I'm wondering what it is. Because the feel is more Boca, you know.
But weren't there some guys that didn't, wouldn't make that transition to electric because it's not cool or it's not, that's not the, the bass, not the true bass sound? Yeah.

Well see what's happening, I don't care too much about playing electric noise now, unless I'm playing rhythm, blues or rock and roll. But when I'm playing jazz, I'm going to play the fiddle. Now if I'm playing rhythm, blues or rock, well I play the, you know. And usually the thing, mostly guitar players make better electric bass players anyway, because they already got that feel, you know, that physical feel, you know. Yeah. The first electric bass I had, I bought it from Walter Payton.
Oh, okay.

Now my son got it in Fort Worth, Texas. Now, you see, Walter Payton wanted to buy it back from me, so he wanted it for sentimental reasons because that's his first electric bass. I said, man, I wanted it for sentimental reasons because it was my first electric bass too. But now my son, he got it in Texas, he won't give it back to me. But he's not learning nothing on it.
I bet it's a Fender, right? Yeah.
Now I've got two other, no it's a Danny Lecter. Is that Dan Electro?
Yeah.

Now I've got two other, I've got two other electric basses, but that's the first one, you know, that I've had. That's when I was playing with Danny White with, you know. Danny Lecter, that's the name.

Yeah, I remember the guitar, Dan Electro, yeah. I remember the guitar, I didn't know they made basses. The Fender was so popular. Yeah, right, sure was. Everybody went out for the Fender in the early 60s. Yeah, right. That was, everybody was out for. Yeah. A little comment on the union, on the musicians' union. Did you have any problems with the union over the years? Earl always had problems with the union.
No, I've been before the board a few times, you know, but it's always ironed out, you know, whatever it was. It wasn't that big, you know.
